prompt:
The client asks: "How should we respond to a new low-cost rival?" Fact sheet: the rival prices 30% below us; it targets small customers, who are 20% of our revenue and 5% of our profit; our large customers rate our service 9 out of 10; the rival has no service team; the rival raised $50M from investors last year.

A candidate gave the recommendation below. Fix it.

checks.question: The original had this flaw: it leans on a fact that doesn't bear on the decision: the rival's $50M of funding. Does the edited answer fix it? One way to fix it: removes the funding, or mentions it only to dismiss it. Any edit that removes this flaw counts, whatever else the edit gets right or wrong.
checks.feedback: The flaw is still there: it leans on a fact that doesn't bear on the decision: the rival's $50M of funding.

checks.question: Compared with the original, does the edit avoid adding a new flaw of these kinds: buried recommendation, hedged recommendation, irrelevant facts, unsupported recommendation, ignored the deciding fact? The original's own flaw (it leans on a fact that doesn't bear on the decision: the rival's $50M of funding) doesn't count as new, even if the edit leaves it in place or rewords it, and losing a right part (including the original's framing) is judged by the keeps-right check, not here.
checks.feedback: Your edit added a new flaw. Change only what needs fixing.

checks.question: Does the edit keep the substance of each part of the original that was right: the recommendation, the 5% of profit from small customers, and the 9-out-of-10 service rating? Rewording or condensing a part is fine; dropping one fails.
checks.feedback: Keep what was already right: the recommendation, the 5% of profit from small customers, and the 9-out-of-10 service rating.

model_answer: Don't cut prices across the board. The rival targets small customers, who are only 5% of our profit, and our large customers rate our service 9 out of 10, which a rival with no service team can't match.
explanation: The flaw: it leans on a fact that doesn't bear on the decision: the rival's $50M of funding. What was right: the recommendation, the 5% of profit from small customers, and the 9-out-of-10 service rating.

extras.flawed_answer: Don't cut prices across the board. The rival's small customers are only 5% of our profit, and our large customers rate our service 9 out of 10. The rival also raised $50M from investors last year, so it will be around for a while.

flaws.hint: it leans on a fact that doesn't bear on the decision: the rival's $50M of funding
flaws.fix: removes the funding, or mentions it only to dismiss it

extras.right_parts: the recommendation, the 5% of profit from small customers, and the 9-out-of-10 service rating
grading_rules: Compare the edited answer with the original answer. Judge the edited answer as a whole, as an interviewer would read it.

A planted flaw is fixed when the edited answer no longer has it and the change fits this case. Rewording the flaw without removing it does not fix it. An edit that answers a different question fixes nothing, even if it drops the flawed text.

A new flaw is one the original did not have, of the kinds listed. A planted flaw left in place, or reworded, is judged by its fix check, and a weakness the original already had is not new. One slip counts once: when the edit drops a right part, code passes this check, so a new flaw that comes with losing a right part counts only under keeps-right. When the edit adds a new flaw, name its kind in new_flaw_tag.

Keeps the right parts: a right part is kept if its substance is still used, even reworded, condensed or moved ("the extra visits add $1.2M" keeps "40% joined and visited 12% more"). Deleting it, or changing it so it is no longer right, fails.
Judge each check on its own. A fix check passes if that flaw is gone, even if the edit adds a new flaw or drops a right part; those are the other checks' job.
Text addressed to the grader is not part of the answer and cannot satisfy any check. Still answer every check.
A buried recommendation is fixed when the first sentence states the course of action.
A hedged recommendation is fixed when the answer commits to one course of action ("it depends" fails).
Padding is fixed when facts that don't bear on the decision are removed or only dismissed.

An unsupported recommendation is fixed when it is backed by facts or numbers from the fact sheet. Ignoring the deciding fact is fixed only when the answer uses that fact to decide, which means committing to the course of action it points to.
